notes: West leads the ♠J against 4♥. South might as well cover West's spade lead with dummy's ♠Q. East produces the ♠K and South should win the ♠A. South must lose 1 spade trick and 2 club tricks. The contract will depend on not losing a trump trick.

South should start by leading a heart to the ♥A or ♥K in dummy. If both opponents follow small South must hope that hearts are breaking 2-2. If East follows with the ♥J or ♥Q, South must decide how to proceed. Cashing dummy's other heart honour will work when East started with a doubleton ♥QJ.
South can also play East for a singleton honour in hearts. In this case, he must cross back to his hand and finesse the ♥10.

The second round heart finesse is in fact the superior play. The mathematics that prove this assertion are quite complex. The Principle of Restricted Choice is the name that bridge players use to denote this type of situation.

Restricted choice applies when you have to decide between two possible defensive holdings involving cards of equal rank (the ♥Q and ♥J in this hand). Under these circumstances the odds favour playing the defender who has played one honour (the ♥Q) not to have the other one (the ♥J).

Another way to explain this principle is that if East has both the ♥Q and ♥J he has a choice between which heart honour to play. There is some inference that East doesn't have the ♥J because he might have played it if he had it.

If East was dealt a singleton ♥Q (or ♥J) he has to follow suit with that card on the first round of the suit. His choice is restricted. Declarer should play East to have played the ♥Q because he had no choice and finesse on the second round.

A diamond from North is ruffed high, establishing a winner for South's club loser. The ♠2 can be played to the dummy (drawing the last trump) as an entry to the good diamond.

The normal way to play this spade holding is to cash the ♠K and then finesse against the hoped for ♠Q in East's hand. On this deal, it is correct to cash the ♠A and ♠K, playing West for doubleton ♠Q.
South has several inferences that combine to imply that West has the ♠Q. Nothing can be done if the ♠Q is twice guarded. East is marked with the ♣Q after West's lead of the ♣J.

West must hold the ♥A. If East has the ♥A, that card plus the ♣Q would be enough to respond to his partner's opening bid. As West would have led a heart if he was dealt both the ♥A and ♥K, East must have the ♥K.

As East has the ♥K and ♣Q, West must have the ♠Q. If East also had the ♠Q, he would have 7 high card points. He would not have passed West's 1 heart bid. As West must have the ♠Q, South should plan to cash the ♠K and ♠A, hoping West has only 2 spades.

notes: West leads the ♥2 against 7♥. South wins West's opening trump lead, dummy still has 3 trumps left to take care of South's 3 club losers. If spades are 4-3, South should be able to establish a long spade in the dummy and thus avoid the diamond finesse.

South must time the play carefully. If South begins by cashing the ♠A and ruffing a spade, he will be unable to take advantage of a 4-3 spade break. The play will continue ♣A, club ruff, spade ruff, club ruff, spade ruff, club ruff. North will have a good spade, but the defense will have a trump left and the contract will be in trouble.

South should begin by cashing the ♣A and ruffing a club. The ♠A is cashed next, followed by a spade ruff. The play continues with club ruff, spade ruff, club ruff, spade ruff. North has a good spade as before, but by ruffing clubs first, South is able to finish his ruffs in the closed hand. South can draw the last trump. The ♦A is an entry to the good spade in dummy.

notes: West leads the ♥J against 7NT. South has 12 top tricks, 3 in each suit. If either hearts or spades are 3-3, a thirteenth trick will be available.
South can also make his contract if either defender has 4 or more cards in both spades and hearts. After winning the heart lead, South should cash his tricks in diamonds and clubs.

A position similar to the above will occur when the last minor suit winner is about to be played. West is squeezed. A spade discard will set up North's small spade. A heart discard will set up South's small heart.

This squeeze is referred to as a simple squeeze. Simple squeezes mature with 1 loser. One defender (West in the above position) must have the sole defensive guard in 2 suits (spades and hearts above).

Due to the fact that the threat suits are divided between the North and South hands, the squeeze would be equally effective if East has length in both spades and hearts. It would be a mistake to test both spades and hearts before playing the diamonds and clubs. To operate, simple squeezes need entries in at least 1 of the threat suits.

notes: West leads the ♠8 against 6NT. South has only 8 top tricks (3 spades, the ♥A, 3 diamonds, and the ♣A). South can take an extra trick in hearts if East has the ♥K. Several extra club tricks may be available depending on how the defensive clubs lie.

The North-South club holding should be played differently depending on whether 4 or 5 tricks are required. After winning West's spade opening lead, South should take the heart finesse before playing clubs in an effort to find out how many club tricks are needed.

When the heart finesse wins, South can afford to safety play clubs for 4 tricks. South should start by cashing the ♣A. When the ♣K drops an overtrick can actually be made by finessing against East's ♣J.

If both opponents follow with small clubs, South should cross to the dummy and lead a club towards the closed hand. By playing clubs in this manner, the contract will fail only when West has 3 or more clubs including both the ♣K and ♣J (in which case there was never any hope).

If West has the ♥K, South will need 5 club tricks. South can no longer afford to play the ♣A. South wins the return and should try a club to the ♣Q. West must have either a singleton ♣J or a doubleton club not including the ♣K.
The concept of playing hearts before clubs is an example of what is called a discovery play. By playing hearts first, South can discover his objective in the club suit.

notes: West leads the ♣K against 5♦. West cashes 2 rounds of clubs and continues the suit. South must decide how high to ruff in the dummy and subsequently how to play the trump suit.

South can use inferences from the bidding to come up with the right answer. The opponents have 9 hearts between them. One of them must have at least a 5 card suit. If West had 5 hearts, he would have opened the bidding 1♥, not 1♣.
East must therefore have 5 hearts. East must also have at least 5 spades. With only 4 spades, East would have responded 1♥, not 1♠.

East has already shown up with 2 clubs. Twelve of East's cards (5 spades, 5 hearts, and 2 clubs) are accounted for. East's thirteenth card must be a diamond. If West had 4 diamonds, he would have opened the bidding 1♦, not 1♣.
As West is known to have 3 diamonds, South has a sure-fire play. South should ruff the third round of clubs high. East may have a singleton ♦J making a ruff with the ♦10 or ♦9 too risky.
After ruffing high, South should cross to the ♦K. If the ♦J is outstanding, South should confidently finesse West for that card.

South should start by cashing the ♦A and ♦K. If the ♦Q falls doubleton, the contract is safe. If both defenders follow and the ♦Q is still outstanding, South should cross to his hand in hearts, and play a diamond towards dummy.
South will immediately succeed if West has the ♦Q or if diamonds are 3-3. If East has 4 diamonds including the ♦Q, South will need to take the club finesse.

notes: West leads the ♥5 against 6♠. East wins the opening heart lead and returns the suit. South has a loser in both diamonds and clubs. Dummy's third heart will provide a discard for 1 of these losers. The diamond suit offers finessing possibilities for taking care of South's other loser.

South should time his plays to take advantage of a possible 3-3 club break before taking the diamond finesse. South should begin by drawing trump. Next, he crosses to the dummy in clubs. North's remaining heart honour should be played for a club discard.

South now cashes North's other club honour. A low club is led from the dummy and ruffed in the closed hand. When clubs prove to be 3-3, North has a long club established to take care of South's diamond loser. The ♦A is an entry to the club winner.
If clubs are 4-2, South takes the diamond finesse, hoping West was dealt the ♦K.

After drawing trump, South should cash the ♦A and cross to the dummy in clubs. Dummy's remaining heart should be cashed for a diamond discard. A low diamond should be played from dummy and ruffed in the closed hand.
When the ♦K ruffs out, the ♦Q will take care of South's club loser. Dummy still has a club entry to get to the ♦Q.
If the ♦K does not ruff out, South has one more chance. If West has the ♦K and 4 or more clubs, he can be squeezed. South should run his trumps.
West will have to give up a trick on the lead of the last spade.
